According to all reports which come to my ears, our Fraternity is doing well. In fact it
is doing quite well. All 20,000-plus of us who have known the active undergraduate
experience have watched for progress
�
and we've seen it over the past few years.
There is no reason to believe that progress will not continue to be the watchword
from now on. It is in the cards. Two Chapters which departed during the difficult days
at many undergraduate institutions of higher learning during the late 1960's and early
1970's have been reactivated. Looking back over the years, we beheve that unsettled
period is not apt to appear again for a considerable time. Hence there is every reason to
believe that we shall move ahead, and this movement may occur faster than we think.
What has been written would not have been put on paper were it not substantiated
by facts worth considering. Think of it �
not too many years back the Annual Giving
Program raised a total of little more than $25,000. Last year it rose to over $63,000,
with more givers than ever. This progress is continuing during the 1979-80 period as
well. It has been reported that giving has exceeded the point reached last year at the
time ofthis writing, and �
more important
�
there are more brothers who have given
for the first time or who have given again after many years of not giving.
All of this bodes well for the regular operations of our Fraternity. It means that the
international office can function better and be of even more service to the Chapters.
Our two reactivated Chapters at the University of Wisconsin and at McGill University
in Montreal are still in need of special attention while working their way back into the
fold. There is a budding Chapter developing at Tufts, and the Nu Chapter at the
University of Toronto will soon be reactivated.
Should there ever be a question of why we need to expand the appeal of the Annual
Giving Program, perhaps these few examples may give us all a clue. The workload is
increasing. The demand is getting heavier. The cost ofeither or both is not going down.
So much for that. Now let's revert to the last issue of the Psi Upsilon Diamond,
wherein Owlie talked about the Endowment Fund. There is no need to refer to what
was therein contained except to state that real growth is not beyond the reach of us to
attain by 1983. For the last two years the international office has operated without a loss
for the first time since the idea of central administration was developed some years
back.
The Endowment Fund serves a very different purpose from the Annual Giving
Program. The Endowment Fund could provide the Fraternity with the wherewithal to
do all sorts of things which cannot be done at the present time. One million dollars,
properly invested, should produce more than $80,000 of income per year. Perhaps a
new Chapter has been established on some campus and now needs to acquire a better
or more suitable house. The Endowment Fund could provide all or part of the money
needed for that purpose. A sizable endowment also would permit the expenditure of
funds for the founding of Chapters on the campuses of many of our finest universities
where Psi Upsilon is not now represented.
Think about what you can do. Talk it over with your attorney, your banker, and your
wife. Then do what you would have wanted Psi Upsilon alumni to do when you were an
undergraduate of a Chapter. It is not difficult and, as the farmer said, "It gives a lot of
satisfaction."

The 136th Convention was drawing to a
close, and a
group of delegates were dis

no!," gasped one delegate. "Four days?
We've barely survived this year's Con
vention, and it's lasted only three!"
Right he was. The Mu Chapter's edi
tion of the Fraternity's annual Conven
tion, August 22-25, 1979, proved to be an
intensive three days of business and plea
sure. The records of the daily meetings
reflect the progress achieved. The tired,
but satisfied, looks on the faces departing
from Minneapolis that final morning in
August bore testimony to the good times
shared by Psi U brothers.
The Normandy Inn in downtown Min
neapolis served as the home and meeting
place for the 1979 Convention. We all
were together, and the excellent service
helped us to maximize our time at work.
The result was sound legislation: the Con
vention, in one action, directed the Office
of the Executive Council to change its
title to the "International Office" to add
visibility to our
Fraternity's international
character. In another area a detailed
statement regarding the steps Psi U is to
take towai-d the reactivation and expan
sion of Chapters was presented and en
dorsed.

the TrinitN Chapter, in order that the
Fraternit> ma\ join in celebrating the

raising the one-time membership fee

taxes from S25 to $30 for each active mem
ber was
approved in decisive fashion.

budget, with salary increases for the sec

on
Thursday, August 23. Actually, the

problems of mutual concern. Later, four
workshops were scheduled, and these
proved to be another high point in the
proceedings. Recent graduates led semi
nars on the role of the Chapter president,
on alumni relations, rushing, and pledge
education.
After all the talk everyone was thirsty
(and that included the abstainers). Those
who weren't thirsty were tired, and nap
time was allowed for one afternoon and
one evening. Of course, before lunch
there was time for a bob or two. In this
connection what better place is there to
satisfy the thirsties and the hungries than
a pizzeria? After Thursday evening's Ex
ecutive Council meeting we hopped on
the bus to a Psi U-owned and staffed piz
za, beer and hoagie emporium. Immense
quantities of food and beverages were
consumed by brothers young and old.
Every night the undergraduates
seemed to end up at the Chapter House.
The Mu provided all the ingredients for a
good time, even including some dates.
The beer was going down faster than any
thing else, except for perhaps the couples
"gatoring" on the dance floor. Many visit
ing brothers demonstrated their exper
tise in this rare dance maneuver.
Area alumni were invited to Friday's
luncheon. Honorary Convention Cochairman, Bob Brooks, Mu '12 and Bar
nard Jones, Mu '24, gave a hearty wel
come. The bus then left for Lake Minnetonka, where we spent a sunny afternoon
swimming, boating, playing soccer, foot
ball, frisbee, tennis, or just taking in the
scenery. Special entertainment was pro
vided by a dog and soccer ball act. The
Thomas family hosted the occasion, open
ing their beautiful home for all to enjoy.
The food was excellent, and the Miller
beer truck made a guest appearance,
courtesy of Paul Stoddart, Mu '79.
After a full day of deliberations Satur
day came the grand finale. The Min
neapolis Club's main hall was the site of
this year's banquet, just as it had been for
a Psi Upsilon Convention some sixty
years ago. Psi U brothers were in full
command of the evening. The sumptuous
dinner commenced with an invocation
led by Rev. B. Anderson McCarthy, Mu
'66 and spirited singing of our renowned
Psi U songs. Vlany Chapters offered a
tune; then came versions of Dixie, Yank
ee Doodle Dandy and Oh! Canada. An
address by David J. Speer, Mu '50 round
ed out the program.
This was a fulfilling Convention. Often
we would see a delegate writing madly to
complete a resolution for the next meet
ing, and many committees met after
hours. The pace did vary; there still was
time for a dip in the Inn's pool or whirl
pool bath. Alumni parties were held. The
Chapter House was in beautiful shape,
and the newly refurbished bar was the
center of intense beveraging.
This success story is due primarily to
two men, and to those who worked with
them. It was Bob Morey's final Conven
tion as President of the Executive Coun
cil. He followed the schedule rigorously,
and this resulted in efficient meetings.
His warm regard for all Psi U's was infec
tious.
Bill Schilling, Mu '36, President of the
Alumni Association of Minnesota, was the
Convention Chairman. Not enough good
words can be written about this man,
either. Bill arranged a well-run Conven
tion; his personal supervision made it a
great Convention. Of course he was
backed up by many Mu alumni: Don Ferroni '68, John Hurley '71, Duncan
Leighton '78, and Roger Schelper '71 are
just a few of the Chapter alumni who
pitched in. The undergraduates were
organized by three .\Ius of the Class of
'79; Reid Leighton, Jim Hallenberg, and
Paul Stoddart.
The Mu Chapter was at its best. The
warm friendship extended by its mem
bers to their visiting brothers was c\ ident
from the first day. The fellowship shared
by all will be remembered long after tiie
last day of the 136th Convention.

1978-79 Gifts Augur Well for New Challenge
They said it couldn't be done �
that Psi Upsilon never
could raise more than $38,000 in annual contributions! But
it had to be done if our Fraternity was to survive. And done it
has been �
increasingly each year
�
since that ominous
forecast of five years ago.
The statistics and lists which follow constitute an honor roll
of some of the most loyal and supportive alumni in the
fraternity world. Every year more brothers step forward to take
a leadership role; every year the average contribution is in
creased; and every year a higher total is raised.
An analysis of last year's giving pattern shows that 33% of
the Fraternity's alumni who contributed in 1978-79 gave
more than they had given previously, 48% gave the same,
and 9% gave less. Alumni contributing for the first time
numbered 10% of the total donors.
Now our alumni are asked to raise their sights still further in
this never-ending spiral of inflation and in the continuing
expansion of services and activities in behalf of our Chapters.
We need $73,240 to balance our budget in 1979-80 and
look for 2,000 alumni participants to accomplish this by
June thirtieth. Encouraging indeed is this year's alumni re
sponse to date. We can do it!
The Executive Council extends its hearty thanks for each
measure of assistance, large and small. Is it any wonder that
we take such great pride, whatever our age, in calling our
selves Psi U's!

The Passing of an Era
Mrs. Margaret L. Warhurst died on
Monday, August 6, 1979, in East Lans
ing, Michigan following a long illness. For
fifteen years, from 1959 to 1974, she had
served as housemother for the Epsilon
Nu Chapter of Psi Upsilon. Her legacy to
a generation of Epsilon Nu's was a rever
ence for tradition and social awareness.
Born and raised in Freuchie, Scotland,
she had come to the United States with
her husband, a professional golfer. Fol
lowing his death, she applied in 1959 for a
position as a fraternity housemother at
Michigan State. At that time the Uni
versity required each fraternity maintain
ing a house to engage a housemother.
This necessity, viewed as a burden by
many fraternities, quickly proved to be
one of the Epsilon Nu's strongest assets.
A handsome, well dressed woman,
cloaked in an air of dignity, Margaret
Warhurst maintained a tone and standard
of decorum at the Psi Upsilon House
which was acknowledted throughout the
campus.
The beginning of a semester saw her
address each new pledge class regarding
house etiquette. During the 1960's and
1970's, an era of profound change on most
college campuses, the Epsilon Nu main
tained the tradition of dressing with coat
and tie for dinner, a tradition still carried
on
today.
During her tenure as housemother.
dinner was served promptly at the same
time each evening. The brothers took
turns escorting Mrs. Warhurst from her
suite at the head of the stairs on the first
floor to the dining room below, followed
by the rest of the Chapter. When the
brothers were assembled in the dining
room, the doxology was sung. The rare
brother arriving late for dinner first
offered his apologies to Mrs. Warhurst
before asking for permission to be seated.
Following the meal each brother stood
while Mrs. Warhurst's chair was held and
she stood. The entire Chapter then joined
in singing a Psi Upsilon song before leav
ing the dining room, led by Mrs.
Warhurst and her escort.
No formal party at the House ever was
complete without the brothers serenad
ing Mrs. Warhurst. An avid bridge play
er, her company regularly was sought as a
willing fourth. During the 1960's she
served as President of the Michigan State
University Housemothers Association.
Upon her retirement in 1974 Mrs.
Warhurst was elected to membership in
the Epsilon Nu, the only woman ever so
honored by the Chapter. She was the last
active housemother serving a fraternity at
Michigan State, having been retained by
the Chapter long after the University
withdrew its requirement for house
mothers in fraternity houses.
She continued to return to the House
for dinner every Monday evening until
she became ill in the spring of 1979. A
resolution honoring Mrs. Warhurst for
her devotion and service to the Fraternity
was adopted by the delegates to the last
Convention in Minneapolis.
It was fitting that undergraduate
brothers should serve as pallbearers at
her funeral. The Epsilon Nu's first floor
library has been named in her memory,
and a plaque has been placed there for
permanent display.
